mcqs.question: What does the `available` quantity on a StockLevel row represent?
options: onHand minus reserved — the stock that is actually free to promise to a new order
The total quantity ever received into the warehouse, including sold units
The physical count currently sitting on the shelf, regardless of pending orders
The quantity currently in transit between two warehouses
mcqs.explanation: Available is specifically what's left to sell after subtracting stock already committed to pending orders (reserved) from what physically exists (onHand). Physical shelf count alone is onHand, not available; total-ever-received and in-transit quantities are different concepts entirely.

mcqs.question: A warehouse has 100 units on hand and 30 reserved against pending orders. If the system only tracked one 'quantity' field instead of separating on-hand from reserved, what goes wrong?
options: Nothing — a single field is mathematically equivalent as long as it's updated correctly
The 30 reserved units would still appear sellable to new orders, since there's no field capturing that they're already committed, leading to oversell
The warehouse would be unable to receive any new stock
Reservations would automatically expire after 24 hours
mcqs.explanation: Without separating reserved from on-hand, there's no way to represent 'physically present but already promised' — new orders would see the full 100 as sellable and could claim units already committed elsewhere, causing oversell. A single field is not equivalent because it can't express partial commitment, and this has nothing to do with receiving new stock or automatic expiry.

mcqs.question: Two orders for the last unit of a SKU arrive nearly simultaneously. What prevents both from successfully reserving it?
options: Rate-limiting orders to one per customer per minute
Displaying a 'low stock' warning in the UI
Folding the availability check and the reservation write into a single atomic conditional update, so only one request's update can match the current row state
Processing all orders for a SKU in a single background thread once per day
mcqs.explanation: An atomic conditional update evaluates the check against the true current row and applies the write together, so only one of two racing requests can succeed — the other affects zero rows and is treated as out of stock. Rate-limiting, UI warnings, and daily batch processing don't close the race window at write time and would be far too slow for real-time checkout.

mcqs.question: What is the main operational cost of pooling availability across nearby warehouses instead of reserving at a single location?
options: It eliminates the need for a StockLevel entity entirely
It makes oversell impossible under any concurrency pattern
It removes the need for reservations altogether
It requires deciding which specific warehouse actually fulfills an order, factoring in shipping cost and time between candidates
mcqs.explanation: Pooling reduces stockouts shown to customers but adds real complexity: once multiple warehouses could fulfill an order, something has to decide which one actually ships it, typically weighing shipping cost and delivery time. StockLevel and reservations are still needed per warehouse, and pooling doesn't remove the concurrency risk — it just changes what's being checked.
